title: Game of Life
directAnswer: Apply Conway's four rules to every cell simultaneously. The naive answer copies the board so reads aren't polluted by writes (O(mn) space). The interview answer encodes the next state in a second bit IN PLACE: keep the current state in bit 0, write the next state into bit 1, read neighbors with `cell & 1`, then in a final pass right-shift every cell. O(mn) time, O(1) extra space.

remember.pattern: In-place 2-bit state encoding (next state in the high bit)
rules: Update must be **simultaneous** — every cell's next state depends only on the CURRENT generation, so you can't overwrite cells in place naively.
Encode two generations in two bits: **bit 0 = current**, **bit 1 = next**. Read neighbors with `cell & 1`, write next with `cell |= 2`.
Because you only ever **set** bit 1 (never touch bit 0) in the first pass, neighbor reads stay correct throughout.
Do a **second pass** that does `cell >>= 1` to promote the next state to the current state.
Only **count live neighbors equal to 1 in bit 0** — encoded values 2 or 3 still read as their original current state via `& 1`.

remember.takeaway: The reusable trick is storing the NEXT state in unused high bits so the CURRENT state survives for neighbor reads, then doing a cleanup pass to shift. It generalizes to any in-place simultaneous-update grid problem — the key realization is that one int can hold two generations at once.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you see that the update is simultaneous (a classic correctness trap) and whether you can achieve O(1) extra space by encoding the next state without destroying the current state needed by neighbors.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Updating cells in place with plain 0/1, so cells processed earlier corrupt the neighbor counts of cells processed later; or counting neighbors with == 1 after some have been overwritten with the next state.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the simultaneity constraint first, give the O(mn)-copy baseline, then derive the 2-bit in-place encoding and mention the infinite-board follow-up handled with a hash set of live coordinates.

problemStatement:
The board is an `m x n` grid of cells, each either live (`1`) or dead (`0`). Each cell interacts with its eight neighbors (horizontal, vertical, diagonal) using the following rules (applied ***simultaneously*** to every cell):

1. Any live cell with fewer than two live neighbors dies (under-population).
2. Any live cell with two or three live neighbors lives on.
3. Any live cell with more than three live neighbors dies (over-population).
4. Any dead cell with exactly three live neighbors becomes a live cell (reproduction).

The next state is created by applying the above rules simultaneously to every cell in the current state. Given the current state of the `board`, update it **in place** to reflect its next state.

***Follow-up:*** Could you solve it in place? Remember the board needs to be updated simultaneously. And what about the board being infinite?
understanding: Every cell's fate is decided by counting its (up to) eight live neighbors in the CURRENT generation, then applying Conway's rules. The catch is simultaneity: all cells transition together, so we must not let an already-updated cell influence the neighbor count of a cell we haven't processed yet. The challenge is doing this update in place without an O(mn) copy.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do all cells update simultaneously based on the current generation?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. That's the central constraint — each cell looks only at the current state of its neighbors, not at any already-computed next states. This is why I can't naively overwrite cells with 0/1 as I go.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are out-of-grid neighbors treated as dead?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — cells beyond the board edges count as dead (0). I'll bounds-check each of the eight offsets.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is O(1) extra space required, or is an O(mn) copy acceptable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: An O(mn) copy is the simplest correct solution, but the follow-up asks for in-place. I'll present both and lead the optimization with a 2-bit encoding.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if the board were infinite?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Then a dense matrix is infeasible. I'd store only the coordinates of live cells in a hash set and tally neighbor counts over live cells and their neighbors — I can sketch that as the follow-up.

approaches.name: Copy the Board (baseline, O(mn) space)
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to nail correctness — it sidesteps the simultaneity trap cleanly before you optimize space.
hints: The danger is that updating a cell to its next value changes the neighbor count seen by cells you process later. How do you guarantee every cell reads the ORIGINAL generation?
Make a full copy of the board first. Read neighbor counts from the (immutable) copy; write the next state into the original board.
Because reads and writes target different arrays, order of processing no longer matters — the update is effectively simultaneous.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Visit each of mn cells, count up to 8 neighbors (constant) → O(mn) time. The snapshot copy uses O(mn) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
The whole difficulty of Game of Life is the word **simultaneously**. If you overwrite a cell with its next value while scanning, a neighboring cell you visit afterward will count the *new* value instead of the *current* one, producing a wrong generation. The simplest way to guarantee correctness is to physically separate the two generations.

**How the copy removes the trap.** Take a complete snapshot of the board before doing any updates. Then, for each cell, count its live neighbors by reading the **snapshot** (which never changes) and write the resulting next state into the **original** board. Because every neighbor read comes from the frozen copy, it doesn't matter what order we process cells in or which originals we've already overwritten — the reads always reflect the current generation. This is the textbook 'double buffering' technique used in graphics and simulations.

**Why it's worth presenting even though it isn't optimal.** It is unambiguously correct and easy to reason about, so it's the right first thing to say in an interview — it proves you understand the simultaneity requirement before you start being clever about space. Many candidates jump straight to an in-place hack, make a subtle ordering mistake, and can't explain why it's wrong. Leading with the copy shows disciplined thinking.

**Its only weakness.** It uses `O(mn)` auxiliary memory for the snapshot. The follow-up explicitly asks to do it in place, which motivates the bit-encoding approach. But on a `25 × 25` board the copy is perfectly acceptable in practice — the optimization is about demonstrating you *can* avoid the copy, not about a real performance need here.
approaches.insight: Double buffering — read from a frozen snapshot, write to the live buffer — is the universal cure for 'all cells update at once' bugs. When in doubt about an in-place simultaneous update, reach for the copy first to lock in correctness, then optimize space only if asked.

approaches.name: In-Place 2-Bit Encoding (Optimal, O(1) space)
approaches.whenToMention: The follow-up answer. Explain the bit layout (bit0=current, bit1=next) before writing code.
hints: You don't need a whole copy — you only need to remember each cell's CURRENT value while also recording its NEXT value. A single int has spare bits. Could you store both?
Use bit 0 for the current state and bit 1 for the next state. Count neighbors with (cell & 1) so you always read the current generation, and record the next state with cell |= 2.
After processing every cell, do a second pass that right-shifts each cell (cell >>= 1) to drop the old current bit and promote the next-state bit.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two passes over mn cells, each counting ≤ 8 neighbors → O(mn) time. We reuse the board's own integers to hold two generations, so only O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
The copy works but spends `O(mn)` memory just to remember the old generation. The key realization is that we don't need a *separate* board to hold the next generation — each cell is an `int` with plenty of unused bits, so we can pack **both** generations into one cell.

**The bit layout.** Reserve **bit 0** (the ones place) for the *current* state and **bit 1** (the twos place) for the *next* state. Initially every cell is `0` or `1`, so bit 1 is `0` everywhere. There are four encoded values: `00` = dead→dead, `01` = live→dead, `10` = dead→live, `11` = live→live. The crucial property is that `cell & 1` always recovers the *current* state, and `cell >> 1` recovers the *next* state.

**Why neighbor reads stay correct.** During the first pass we only ever **set** bit 1 (`cell |= 2`); we *never modify bit 0*. So no matter how many neighbors we've already 'updated', counting live neighbors with `neighbor & 1` always returns their original current-generation value. That's exactly the simultaneity guarantee the copy gave us — achieved without extra memory, because the old value is preserved untouched in bit 0 while the new value accumulates in bit 1. This is the single insight that makes the in-place solution correct.

**Applying the rules.** For each cell, count live neighbors `live` using `& 1`. If the cell is currently live (`cell & 1 == 1`) and `live` is 2 or 3, it survives, so set its next bit: `cell |= 2`. If the cell is currently dead and `live == 3`, it reproduces, so again `cell |= 2`. In every other case the next state is dead, and since bit 1 starts at `0` we simply leave it alone — no clearing needed.

**The cleanup pass.** After all cells carry their next state in bit 1, a second sweep does `cell >>= 1` on every cell. This discards the now-irrelevant current bit and shifts the next-state bit down into bit 0, leaving a clean `0`/`1` board representing the new generation. Two passes, no auxiliary array.

**Why this is the canonical in-place answer.** It's the textbook resolution to the follow-up: it keeps time at `O(mn)`, drops space to `O(1)`, and the bit trick generalizes to any simultaneous-update grid where the state set is small enough to encode in spare bits. Mentioning that you could also encode richer transitions (e.g., distinct codes for 'was-live-now-dead') shows command of the technique.
approaches.insight: An integer cell can carry two generations at once: low bit = now, high bit = next. Because neighbor counting only reads the low bit and updates only set the high bit, the current generation is never disturbed mid-pass — that's the in-place version of double buffering, paid for in bits instead of bytes.

pitfalls: Counting neighbors with == 1 instead of & 1 — once a neighbor is encoded as 3, == 1 misses it.
Forgetting the final >>= 1 pass — board stays in encoded form.
Clearing bit 0 during the first pass — destroys the current state other cells still need.
Using values that overflow two bits (e.g., +=) — stick to bitwise OR for the next-state flag.

commonMistakes: Updating cells in place with plain 0/1 — earlier writes corrupt later neighbor counts (the simultaneity bug).
Counting live neighbors with == 1 after some cells were re-encoded — use & 1.
Forgetting the final right-shift pass that promotes the next state.
Treating out-of-bounds neighbors as live instead of dead.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: In-place update without encoding (the simultaneity bug)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Overwriting board[i][j] with the next 0/1 means a later cell counts this cell's NEW value as a neighbor, not its current value, producing a wrong generation.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Counting neighbors with == 1 instead of & 1
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Once a neighbor has its next-state bit set it becomes 2 or 3. Comparing == 1 then misses currently-live cells encoded as 3, undercounting neighbors.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting the shift-down pass
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After the first pass the board holds encoded values (0,1,2,3). Without the final cell >>= 1, the output is the two-bit encoding, not the next generation.

patternNote: In-place simultaneous grid update via spare-bit encoding (next state in the high bit) plus a cleanup shift pass. Recognise it whenever every cell must update at once from neighbors' current values AND O(1) space is demanded. The copy/double-buffer is the correctness baseline; the bit trick is the space optimization. For an infinite board, switch to a hash set of live coordinates.
